title: Heritage Bookbinding Elements Transform in Contemporary Sculptures by Adelene Koh
description: After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in J
body:
After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in Japan, then led her to London, and she’s now based in Taiwan, where she runs a studio called dddots. This year, Koh was one of 30 finalists for the Loewe Foundation Craft Prize, which celebrates innovation across a wide range of artisanship.
As a bookmaker and conservator, Koh draws upon the technical precision and heritage of bookmaking to create unique sculptures using paper and thread. Her work “Endless” was included in the prize’s exhibition of shortlisted artists, consisting of a kind of ouroboros-like cylinder of meticulously folded paper and edges stitched with colorful fiber. “The result is an endless loop of a book’s spine and fore-edge bound together by the English endband sewing techniques from the 18th and 19th centuries,” says a statement.

Sewn endbands are not exactly invisible, but they’re usually tucked snugly inside the cover. The thread is also not necessarily colorful, as it may be selected to blend in with the pages or other parts of the binding. For Koh, this underappreciated element becomes the highlight through vibrant combinations and rhythmic patterns. “I’m interested in bringing hidden elements of books into focus,” Koh says. “I’m drawn to the overlooked, the sidelined, the parts that quietly support everything else.”
The winner of this year’s competition is Jongjin Park, and Colossal readers may also recognize the work of finalist Xanthe Somers. See more on Koh’s Instagram.

title: V&A Storehouse Workers Vote to Strike Over “Amazon-Style” Conditions
description:
News
                Staff members allege they were “denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks.”
body:
News
                Staff members allege they were “denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Victoria and Albert (V&A) East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage site in East London (photo 14GTR via Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0)
    
        
            Unionized workers at the Victoria and Albert (V&A) East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage site, have voted unanimously to strike over alleged "Amazon-style" working practices.On Wednesday, July 29, all of the Storehouse employees who voted in a union ballot said they would go on strike, citing being "denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks," according to a press release shared by Prospect, the union that represents them. The union is demanding that the museum give employees two paid breaks per day, a request it said the museum has failed to adopt.

title: The Thorny Politics of Protest Photography
description:
Film Review
                A new documentary follows the work of activist and photographer Misan Harriman, but risks overly aes
body:
Film Review
                A new documentary follows the work of activist and photographer Misan Harriman, but risks overly aestheticizing the movements he captures.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Still from Misan Harriman: Shoot the People (2026), dir. Andy Mundy-Castle (all images courtesy Watermelon Pictures)
    
        
            In a 2013 essay, author Barrett Swanson asked, “At what point does the aesthetic excellence of the photograph eclipse the depicted event, or, worse, distract the viewer from inquiring into what happened?” With the synchronous explosion of digital news content and unremitting global calamity, it’s a question that strongly resonates today, particularly with photography of protest and social movements. If these images overtly flatter the protestor, they can be accused of fueling performative activism and pulling attention away from the crisis at hand; if they are too beautiful, they might conceal the real risk of violence from the state. Still, if they are too graphic, they can rob the subjects of their dignity, making a cheap spectacle of dissidence.These are tensions of which photographer-activist Misan Harriman, who has rapidly made a name for himself documenting protests since the summer of 2020, is no doubt keenly aware.Harriman is the subject of Andy Mundy-Castle’s new documentary Shoot the People, which follows the 48-year-old Nigerian-born Brit as he chronicles activist movements across three continents. While Harriman's evolution from an amateur photographer to the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of Vogue's September edition is impressive, more exigent is his artful representation of protests, especially (though not exclusively) those in which primarily Black and Brown people are filling the streets.

title: Long-Contested Guggenheim Abu Dhabi Gets Opening Date
description:
News
                Activists have called on artists to boycott the new museum, citing inhumane treatment of workers.
body:
News
                Activists have called on artists to boycott the new museum, citing inhumane treatment of workers. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Exterior of the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim Abu Dhabi (all images courtesy Guggenheim Abu Dhabi)
    
        
            After 20 years of delays, allegations, and recalibrations, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation will open the doors to its Frank Gehry-designed Abu Dhabi outpost on December 11. The 30-gallery museum will join seven other cultural institutions on Saadiyat Island, including the Zayed National Museum and Berklee Abu Dhabi."The museum’s art collection is uniquely local and global, centred in the region but with works from all continents," Guggenheim Director and CEO Mariët Westermann said in a statement. She expressed that the museum will showcase the "experimental character of art since 1960," including abstractions, storytelling, painting, and moving images. In the past 16 years, the art activism group Gulf Labor Coalition (GLC) has been calling attention to abuse allegations of migrant workers and violations of local and international labor laws linked to the new museum. In 2015, an offshoot of the group called Gulf Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.) staged a May Day occupation of the Guggenheim Museum in New York and a May 8 occupation of the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice during the Venice Biennale. On May Day 2015, members of the Gulf Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.) unveiled a large parachute in the Guggenheim Museum rotunda with the words “Meet Workers Demands Now” (photo Benjamin Sutton/Hyperallergic)"None of the initial reasons for this action have been adequately resolved over the years, despite Gulf Labor's strident efforts, and the art world's generally sympathetic response," GLC Co-Founder Andrew Ross told Hyperallergic after this week's announcement about the December opening.The Guggenheim Museum and Foundation has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

title: How a Former Military Settlement in Taipei Became an Artist Residency
description:
Feature
                Treasure Hill served as a Japanese ammunition depot and Kuomintang squatter settlement prior to its reop
body:
Feature
                Treasure Hill served as a Japanese ammunition depot and Kuomintang squatter settlement prior to its reopening as an artist village in 2010.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A view of Treasure Hill in the outskirts of Taipei (all photos Andrew Nachemson/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            TAIPEI, Taiwan — Two tiny lightbulbs dangle from five feet of wire, blinking on and off to the rhythm of human breath. Magnets attached to the bulbs pull them together or push them apart at random, mimicking the relationships between people — or communities. “I was inspired when I drove by the bridge outside and saw Treasure Hill,” Taiwanese artist Jia-Jhen Syu, whose installation was part of the larger project, “The Third Memorial,” displayed at the artist residency in April and May, told Hyperallergic. Tucked away in a small forested area on the banks of the Xindian River in Taipei City lies the Treasure Hill Artist Village. Founded by retreating soldiers in the 1940s, the former anti-aircraft base turned squatter settlement has been through a number of reincarnations. Its latest form, launched in 2010, is as a so-called “living history,” where the descendants of its original inhabitants live side by side with artists in residence.Artist Jia-Jhen Syu standing beside a sculpture he made from used soap at Treasure Hill in April“Each household has its own story,” Yi-Chen Bai, who was born in Treasure Hill to a Kuomintang foot soldier, said to Hyperallergic. Originally from China’s Hubei province, her father was on the losing side of the Chinese Civil War, which led to the communist overthrow of the Republic of China government — which then retreated to its final stronghold of Taiwan in 1949.Some of the soldiers from the Republic settled in Treasure Hill, which the government viewed as a temporary military camp. It initially tried to prevent the troops from bringing their families with them or building more permanent infrastructure on the site, but its attempts were unsuccessful.

title: California Exhibition to Document One of the US’s Worst Deportation Campaigns
description:
News
                “Help Wanted / Leave Now” traces the infamous “Operation Wetback” implemented by Eisenhower in 1954 to expe
body:
News
                “Help Wanted / Leave Now” traces the infamous “Operation Wetback” implemented by Eisenhower in 1954 to expel undocumented Mexican workers. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
             "Operation Wetback" historian Juan Garcia's mother, Maria de la Luz Perez-Hernandez (photo courtesy Juan Garcia; all other photos courtesy the California Museum)
    
        
            Juan Garcia, history professor emeritus at the University of Arizona, grew up in South Texas in an established Mexican-American ranching family. When he was around six years old, his father abruptly abandoned his trade and relocated his nine children to Chicago.The reasons his family left Texas were complicated, and the retired professor has since spent his career studying the political headwinds that punctuated the lives of his farmer father and his mother, who lived in the United States as an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, as they headed east. Some of the fruits of Garcia's research and excerpts of his family story will be publicly displayed in a forthcoming exhibition at Sacramento's California Museum, entitled Help Wanted / Leave Now: "Operation Wetback" & the Revolving Door of Mass Deportation. Organized in collaboration with historians including Garcia and labor rights activist Dolores Huerta, the bilingual exhibition revolves around "Operation Wetback," one of the US's most notorious operations to deport Mexican immigrants. ("Wetback" was a derogatory term used to refer to undocumented immigrants who may have crossed into the US through the Rio Grande.) The exhibition will open on August 13 and run through January 10, 2027.

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Your remedy against toxic people, Trump’s war against the Smithsonian, and saying goodbye to two giants of the arts.   
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            How many days of your life have been ruined because of someone else's fragile ego? How many times have so-called "friends" shamelessly stolen your ideas? In this month's Art Problems column, Paddy Johnson tackles an uncomfortable question: Why are there so many toxic people in the art world? Read her tips on how to protect yourself from insecure peers and bad-faith actors. Hope it helps. Speaking of toxic people, President Trump has ordered the installation of content warning signs outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History to alert the public against the institution's alleged leftist bias. "No other president has seen fit to vandalize taxpayer-funded museums with a billboard telling people not to go inside, while directing them to more politically 'palatable' — which is to say extreme right-wing — revisions of the historical record," writes Ed Simon in a must-read opinion piece below.In other stories, this week we said goodbye to two giants: assemblage artist Betye Saar, who died just four days before her 100th birthday, and performance artist Simone Forti, who passed away at 91. We mourn their death while celebrating the massive legacies they've left behind.  —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief


	
		
			Madrid Museum Puts Picasso in Dialogue With “African Guernica”
		
	
	
		Spanning over 25-feet wide and 11-feet high, Pablo Picasso’s painting “Guernica” (1937) is as monumental in size as it is in cultural significance. Its startling depiction of state brutality against civilians has made it an emblem of post-war Spanish identity, and its cry against violence has resonated with besieged people worldwide — from Vietnam to Gaza — throughout the past nine decades. 
A new annual exhibition series at the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid, which has served as the canonical work’s permanent home since 1992, places “Guernica” in dialogue with other artworks. The new program, titled History Doesn’t Repeat Itself, but It Does Rhyme, partly aims to revisit the universal political impulses behind the anti-war painting — but its first iteration also exposes race as an urgent issue for contemporary art institutions in Spain. | Agnish Ray
